stages.title: Advanced microeconomics
stages.hook: If a government caps the price of rent below the market level, who gains, who loses, and can the loss be measured?
explain: Consumer surplus is the gap between what buyers are willing to pay and what they actually pay. Producer surplus is the gap between the price sellers receive and the lowest price they would accept. In a competitive market at equilibrium, total surplus (the sum) is as large as possible, which economists call allocative efficiency.

Interventions such as price ceilings, price floors or taxes move the market away from equilibrium. Some trades that would benefit both sides no longer happen. The lost surplus is called deadweight loss. Firms maximise profit where marginal revenue equals marginal cost (MR = MC).

Efficiency is not the only goal. A price ceiling may make housing affordable for some tenants even though it reduces total surplus and may cut supply. Economists measure the trade-off, while the choice depends on values about fairness and who is helped.

example.q: Demand is P = 20 − Q and supply is P = 2 + 2Q (P in zeds). Find equilibrium, consumer surplus and producer surplus.
example.a: Q = 6, P = 14; consumer surplus 18, producer surplus 36

analogies.home: You would pay up to 20 for a book but find it for 14: your surplus is 6.
analogies.farm: A farmer who would sell at 2 but gets 14 gains a surplus of 12 on that item.
analogies.city: Rent controls help current tenants but may reduce the number of flats offered.
analogies.tech: A surge-price cap on rides may lower fares but leave some riders waiting.

stages.mnemonic: CS above price, PS below price; the triangle you lose is the deadweight loss.
terms: Willingness to pay minus price paid.
Price received minus minimum acceptable price.
Total surplus lost when trades that would benefit both do not occur.
Resources produce what people value most, with no way to gain without loss.

misc.wrong: Whatever the market does is automatically fair.
misc.right: Efficiency and fairness are separate. Markets can be efficient yet leave unequal outcomes, which is why people argue about intervention.

stages.limits: Surplus analysis assumes competitive markets, no externalities and that willingness to pay reflects value, which is weaker when incomes differ greatly. Models give directions of effects, not exact forecasts.

trip.prompt: Find the diagram showing consumer and producer surplus and locate deadweight loss from a tax.

questions.q: Consumer surplus is...
o: willingness to pay minus the price paid
the price a firm charges minus the cost of making the good
a firm's revenue minus its total costs
the total amount that buyers spend in a market
questions.why: It is the benefit buyers get beyond the price.

questions.q: Profit-maximising firms produce where...
o: marginal revenue equals marginal cost
price equals zero, so that every unit is given away
average cost is at its highest point
revenue falls to zero for the firm at any output
questions.why: Producing more adds revenue less than cost beyond that point.

questions.q: Demand is P = 20 − Q and supply is P = 2 + 2Q. What is the equilibrium quantity?
questions.why: 20 − Q = 2 + 2Q gives Q = 6.

questions.q: With P = 20 − Q, supply P = 2 + 2Q and equilibrium P = 14, Q = 6, what is the consumer surplus (triangle)?
A price ceiling of 10 is set in that market. Quantity traded is limited by supply: 10 = 2 + 2Q. What quantity is supplied?
questions.why: 2Q = 8 so Q = 4.

questions.q: At Q = 4 the demand price is 16 and the supply price is 10. Deadweight loss is the triangle from Q = 4 to Q = 6. What is its area?
A binding price ceiling set below equilibrium typically causes...
o: a shortage
a surplus
no change
higher quantity supplied
questions.why: Quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at the capped price.

questions.q: Which statement about deadweight loss is correct?
o: It arises when mutually beneficial trades are blocked
It is the profit that a firm makes when it holds a large share of the market
It is the tax revenue the government collects from a sale
It is always zero, whatever the tax rate is set at
questions.why: It measures the lost gains from trade.

questions.q: A government imposes rent controls. Give one argument for and one against.
questions.model: For: it can keep rents affordable and protect current tenants. Against: lower rents can reduce the supply and quality of housing, create shortages and cut total surplus.
questions.why: Both benefits and costs exist.

questions.q: A firm has MR = 12 and MC = 9 at its current output. What should a profit-maximiser do?
o: Increase output
Reduce output
Keep output unchanged
Shut down immediately
questions.why: Each extra unit adds more revenue (12) than cost (9).

panel.q: A tax lowers total surplus yet is widely used. How do economists best explain this?
o: Taxes fund public goods and redistribution, so the lost surplus must be weighed against benefits
Economists think taxes never matter to anyone's choices
Deadweight loss is imaginary and has never been seen in practice
Taxes are free for those who pay them, so there is no loss
panel.why: Deadweight loss is a cost, but the use of revenue may be worth it.

panel.q: Why might maximising total surplus not satisfy everyone's idea of fairness?
panel.model: Total surplus says nothing about who receives it. Willingness to pay depends on income, so the outcome can be efficient yet unequal, and people differ on how much to value fairness against efficiency.
panel.why: Efficiency and equity are distinct.

panel.q: A price floor above equilibrium (such as a minimum price) usually leads to...
o: a surplus of the good
a shortage of the good, as buyers want more than is offered
lower prices for buyers in the market
no effect at all on the amount traded or on the price
panel.why: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at the floor.

teach.model: Consumer surplus is the extra value buyers get beyond what they pay, and producer surplus is the extra sellers get beyond their minimum price. At equilibrium the total is largest. A price cap or tax blocks some trades and the lost gains are the deadweight loss. For example, a cap below equilibrium creates a shortage.

stages.title: National income accounting
stages.hook: If a country builds a factory, buys imported machines and sells goods abroad, how do we avoid counting everything twice?
explain: GDP measures the market value of final goods and services produced within a country in a period. Three approaches should give the same total: output (value added), income (wages, profits, rents) and expenditure. The expenditure approach is GDP = C + I + G + (X − M), where C is household consumption, I is investment, G is government purchases and X − M is net exports.

Only final goods count, to avoid double counting intermediate goods. Transfer payments such as pensions are not in G because nothing is produced in exchange. Nominal GDP uses current prices; real GDP removes price changes using a price index called the GDP deflator: real GDP = nominal GDP ÷ deflator × 100.

GNI adds income earned abroad by residents and subtracts income sent abroad. GDP is useful but excludes unpaid work, informal activity, environmental damage and the distribution of income, so it is not the same as wellbeing.

example.q: In Lorin, C = 600, I = 150, G = 200, X = 120, M = 100 (billions of zeds). Find GDP. If nominal GDP next year is 1,100 and the deflator is 110, find real GDP.
example.a: GDP = 970 billion zeds; real GDP = 1,000 billion

analogies.farm: Counting both the wheat and the flour made from it would double count; count only the final bread.
analogies.city: A city's total output can be added from what firms add, from what people earn, or from what is spent.
analogies.home: A family budget can be viewed by income, spending or what was produced at home.
analogies.tech: A phone's chip is intermediate; the finished phone is final.

stages.mnemonic: C + I + G + (X − M): Consumers, Investors, Government, net eXports.
terms: Market value of final goods and services produced in a country in a period.
Price index showing how prices of all domestic output changed.
GDP plus net income from abroad.

misc.wrong: Imports reduce GDP because they are subtracted in the formula.
misc.right: Imports are subtracted only to remove foreign production already counted in C, I or G. Imports themselves do not reduce domestic output.

stages.limits: GDP counts spending, not wellbeing. Measuring informal and digital activity is difficult, and economists debate alternatives.

trip.prompt: Find the three ways to measure GDP and what is left out.

questions.q: Which is included in G in GDP = C + I + G + (X − M)?
o: Government spending on building a school
A state pension payment made to people who have retired
Interest paid on the government's debt each year
A benefit payment made to someone who is out of work
questions.why: G counts purchases of goods and services, not transfer payments.

questions.q: C = 500, I = 120, G = 180, X = 90, M = 110 (billions). Calculate GDP.
Nominal GDP is 2,200 and the GDP deflator is 110. What is real GDP?
Real GDP rises from 2,000 to 2,080. What is the growth rate in %?
Why are intermediate goods not added separately to GDP?
o: Their value is already in the final product
They are free, so they add nothing to output
They are all imported, so they do not count in GDP
They have no value until a customer buys them
questions.why: Counting both would double count.

questions.q: Which is NOT counted in GDP?
o: Unpaid housework
A new house built
Haircut paid for
A factory machine bought
questions.why: Unpaid household work is not traded in markets.

questions.q: Match each item to its GDP component.
questions.why: Each is a category in the expenditure approach.

questions.q: A country's GDP is 900 and net income from abroad is +40. What is GNI?
questions.why: GNI = GDP + net income from abroad.

questions.q: Explain why nominal GDP can rise even when the economy produces nothing extra.
questions.model: Nominal GDP uses current prices, so if prices rise while the quantity of output stays the same, nominal GDP goes up. Real GDP adjusts for this to show true output change.
questions.why: Nominal values mix price and quantity.

questions.q: A government gives pensions of 50 billion to retirees. How does this affect measured G?
o: It is a transfer, not counted in G directly
It raises G by 50, as the money is spent by the government
It reduces G by 50, as the money leaves the budget
It lowers X by 50, as exports must fall to pay for it
questions.why: Production does not occur in exchange for a transfer; spending later appears in C.

panel.q: Country A has higher GDP per person than country B. Can we say its people are better off?
o: Not necessarily: GDP ignores distribution, unpaid work, environment and leisure
Yes, always, because a higher GDP per person means a better life
No, GDP is meaningless as a measure of anything
Only if country A has more people or a larger area
panel.why: GDP is a useful but partial indicator.

panel.q: Why might GDP per person at market exchange rates understate living standards in a low-price country?
panel.model: At market exchange rates, a low-price country's incomes look small in a foreign currency, though local money buys more, so purchasing power parity adjustments are often used to compare real living standards.
panel.why: Price levels differ between countries.

panel.q: A firm in Lorin is owned by foreign investors who send profits abroad. Which measure falls relative to the other?
o: GNI relative to GDP
GDP relative to GNI
Neither can differ
Both become zero
panel.why: Profits sent abroad are subtracted from GNI but production still counts in GDP.

teach.model: GDP is the value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a period. You can add it up as C + I + G + (X − M). Only final goods count, so nothing is counted twice. Real GDP removes price changes so you can compare years. For example, nominal 1,100 with a deflator of 110 is real 1,000.

points.ask: How do you add it up?
What is the difference between real and nominal?

stages.title: Aggregate demand and supply
stages.hook: When a government spends 20 units on a project, why might total national income rise by more than 20?
explain: Aggregate demand (AD) is total planned spending in an economy at each price level: AD = C + I + G + (X − M). Aggregate supply (AS) is the total output firms are willing to produce. In the short run, AS can slope upward because some prices and wages adjust slowly. In the long run many economists view output as set by productive capacity such as labour, capital and technology.

A rise in AD (from higher confidence, government spending or exports) can raise output and prices. A fall in short-run AS, for example from an energy price shock, can raise prices and cut output at once, called stagflation. Policies aim to stabilise output and prices, but economists disagree on how much they can help and the strength of the effects.

The multiplier says an initial change in spending leads to a larger change in income because one person's spending is another's income. With marginal propensity to consume (MPC), multiplier = 1 ÷ (1 − MPC). Taxes and imports leak money out of the spending chain and reduce the multiplier.

example.q: The MPC is 0.8. Government spending rises by 20 (billion zeds). What is the maximum total rise in income using the simple multiplier?
steps: This is an upper bound because taxes, imports and savings leak.

analogies.farm: A farmer's payment buys tools from a smith, who buys grain from another farmer, and so on.
analogies.city: A new stadium employs builders who spend wages in local shops.
analogies.music: A single note echoes through the hall, each echo smaller than the one before.
analogies.sea: A harbour dredging contract creates work for suppliers and workers who then spend their pay.

stages.mnemonic: One person's spending is another's income: the ripple is the multiplier.
terms: Total planned spending at each price level.
Total output firms will produce at each price level.
Ratio of the change in income to the initial change in spending.
High inflation together with weak growth and high unemployment.

misc.right: It depends on MPC, tax rates and import propensity, and can be smaller when people save more or the economy is near full capacity.

stages.limits: The AD-AS model is a simplified picture. Economists debate how flat the short-run supply curve is and how big real-world multipliers are.

trip.prompt: Look at AD and AS diagrams and note what shifts each curve.

questions.q: Which would shift aggregate demand to the right?
o: Rising consumer confidence
A rise in the cost of oil inputs
A fall in exports
Higher taxes on households
questions.why: More planned spending shifts AD right.

questions.q: MPC = 0.75. What is the simple multiplier?
With MPC = 0.9 and an initial spending rise of 10 billion, what is the maximum total rise in income in billions?
questions.why: Multiplier 10; 10 × 10 = 100.

questions.q: If households save 25% of any extra income and ignore taxes and imports, what is the multiplier?
questions.why: MPS = 0.25 so multiplier = 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4.

questions.q: A sudden rise in oil prices raises firms' costs. The usual short-run result in AD-AS is...
o: higher prices and lower output
lower prices and higher output
no change
higher prices and higher output
questions.why: A left shift in short-run AS.

questions.q: Why is the real multiplier typically smaller than the simple formula suggests?
o: Leakages into taxes, savings and imports
People spend more than they earn at each step
Prices fall at each step, which cancels the effect
Exports rise at each step and raise the final total
questions.why: Each round, part of the money leaks out of domestic spending.

questions.q: Match each event to its AD-AS effect.
questions.why: Shifts depend on what changes spending or capacity.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the multiplier exists.
questions.model: When money is spent, it becomes someone else's income. They spend part of it, which becomes another person's income, so the initial spending leads to a larger total rise in income.
questions.why: Spending chains through the economy.

questions.q: Stagflation is hard for policymakers because...
o: policies that fight inflation can worsen unemployment, and vice versa
prices and output both rise strongly together
there is no unemployment, so the problem is easy to solve
it is rare and harmless, so policymakers can ignore it
questions.why: The usual trade-off is worse.

questions.q: In the long run, which most increases an economy's capacity to produce?
o: Better technology and more skilled workers
A temporary spending boost that fades after a year
Lower consumer confidence among households
A short-lived price cut on one popular good
questions.why: Long-run supply depends on productive capacity.

panel.q: Economists differ on how big fiscal multipliers are. Which is a plausible reason?
o: It depends on spare capacity, interest rates and how people expect policy to continue
Multipliers are fixed constants that never change from one time or place to another
Nobody has ever studied multipliers
They are always zero in every economy
panel.why: Context affects the size.

panel.q: Why can stimulating demand be more effective in a deep recession than when the economy is at full capacity?
panel.model: In a recession there are unemployed workers and idle capacity, so extra demand raises output with little inflation. At full capacity, extra demand mostly pushes up prices.
panel.why: Effects depend on spare capacity.

panel.q: Which statement best describes a supply-side policy?
o: Investment in education and infrastructure to raise productive capacity
A one-off cut in government purchases during a downturn
A rise in the confidence of consumers
A change in the exchange rate and nothing else
panel.why: Supply-side policies expand capacity.

teach.model: Aggregate demand is total planned spending in an economy. If spending rises, firms produce more and incomes rise, and those new incomes are spent again, so the total increase is bigger than the first. The multiplier is 1 divided by (1 minus the MPC). For example, with MPC 0.8 the multiplier is 5.

points.ask: Why does the effect get bigger?
How do you calculate the multiplier?
Why is it smaller in real life?

stages.title: Monetary policy
stages.hook: When a central bank raises its interest rate, why might shops see fewer customers a few months later?
explain: Monetary policy is the use of interest rates and the money supply by a central bank to influence the economy. Central banks often aim for stable inflation (for example around 2%) and, in many countries, also high employment. The main tool is the policy interest rate, which affects the rates banks charge.

Higher interest rates raise the cost of borrowing and the reward for saving, which tends to reduce spending and inflation. Lower rates do the reverse. The effects take time and operate through borrowing, asset prices, exchange rates and expectations. Other tools include buying bonds (quantitative easing) and setting bank reserve requirements.

Banks keep part of deposits as reserves and lend the rest, which creates money. With a reserve ratio r, the maximum money multiplier is 1 ÷ r. The real interest rate is approximately the nominal rate minus inflation. Central bank independence is supported by many economists to avoid short-term political pressure, though critics worry about accountability.

example.q: A bank must hold 10% reserves. A new deposit of 500 zeds is made. What is the maximum total of deposits created? Also, if the nominal rate is 6% and inflation 4%, what is the approximate real rate?
example.a: Up to 5,000 zeds in deposits; real rate about 2%

analogies.home: Making borrowing dearer is like a parent tightening the family's spending allowance.
analogies.farm: If loans for seed cost more, farmers may plant less.
analogies.city: Higher mortgage rates slow house buying.
analogies.tech: A thermostat adjusts heat in response to temperature, as policy adjusts rates to inflation.

stages.mnemonic: Rates up, spending down; rates down, spending up (with a delay).
terms: A public institution that manages a country's money and interest rates.
The key interest rate set by the central bank.
Share of deposits banks must or choose to hold.

misc.wrong: Printing money always creates real wealth.
misc.right: More money chasing the same goods can raise prices. Real wealth needs more goods and services.

stages.limits: The timing and strength of monetary policy are uncertain. Interest rates near zero limit the tool, and economists debate unconventional policies and inflation targets. The money multiplier 1 ÷ r is a textbook upper bound. In practice many banks lend first and settle later, and lending is limited more by capital rules and by demand for loans than by reserves alone.

trip.prompt: Find the main tools of a central bank and how they are meant to work.

o: reduce spending and inflation
raise inflation by making borrowing cheaper for all
raise borrowing by households and firms
increase the money supply so that people spend more
questions.why: Higher rates make borrowing costlier.

Reserve ratio 10%. A new deposit of 800. What is the maximum total of deposits created (including the original)?

Nominal interest 3%, inflation 5%. The real interest rate is...
o: negative, about −2%
positive, about +2%, since inflation is lower than the interest rate
8%, found by adding the two rates together
exactly zero, as the two rates cancel out

questions.q: Why does monetary policy work with a delay?
o: Borrowing, spending and prices adjust slowly
Banks ignore the central bank, so changes take time to be noticed
Interest rates do not matter to spending or prices
Inflation is not affected by monetary policy at all
questions.why: Contracts and decisions respond with lags.

questions.q: Match each tool to its effect.
pairs: Adds money and lowers long-term rates
Cuts the amount banks can lend
questions.why: Each tool changes the cost or amount of credit.

questions.q: Explain why high inflation can lead a central bank to raise interest rates, and name one cost of doing so.
questions.model: Higher rates make borrowing costlier, which lowers spending and demand and eases price pressure. The cost can be slower growth, lower investment and higher unemployment.
questions.why: Anti-inflation policy has costs.

questions.q: Why do many economists favour an independent central bank?
o: It can resist short-term political pressure to stimulate before elections
It never makes mistakes about the economy, so its choices are always right
It sets the taxes that people and firms must pay
It runs the government's budget and decides how it is spent
questions.why: Independence supports credibility, though accountability is needed.

questions.q: If the policy rate is already near zero and the economy is weak, which tool might be considered?
o: Quantitative easing (buying bonds)
Raising rates still higher to slow spending
Banning all loans until the economy recovers
Closing banks that are not performing well
questions.why: Unconventional tools can work when rates cannot fall further.

panel.q: Some argue central banks should target only inflation; others say also employment. What best describes the debate?
o: Different goals involve trade-offs and value judgements
One view is proven, so the debate is over
Banks have no goals, so there is nothing to debate
Inflation and unemployment never conflict, so the targets are the same
panel.why: Mandates reflect choices among competing aims.

panel.q: Why can very low interest rates for a long time raise concerns?
panel.model: Prolonged low rates can encourage heavy borrowing and risk-taking, push up asset prices, hurt savers' returns, and leave the central bank little room to cut further in a crisis.
panel.why: Low rates have side effects.

panel.q: Inflation expectations matter because...
o: if people expect higher prices they may demand higher wages and raise prices, making inflation self-fulfilling
expectations never matter, since only current prices count
they set the exchange rate directly, with no other cause
prices follow only the past, whatever people expect to come
panel.why: Expectations influence behaviour and inflation dynamics.

teach.topic: How a central bank steers the economy
teach.model: A central bank sets a key interest rate. Higher rates make borrowing costlier, so people and firms spend less and inflation tends to ease. Lower rates do the opposite. Banks lend out part of deposits, which creates money. For example, with a 10% reserve ratio, a deposit of 500 can support up to 5,000 in deposits.

points.ask: What does the central bank change?
What does that do to spending and prices?

stages.title: Fiscal policy
stages.hook: In a recession, should a government spend more even if it has to borrow? Economists have argued about this for decades.
explain: Fiscal policy is the use of government spending and taxation to influence the economy. Expansionary fiscal policy (more spending or lower taxes) boosts demand; contractionary policy (less spending or higher taxes) reduces it. Automatic stabilisers, like unemployment benefits and progressive taxes, adjust without new decisions.

The budget deficit is spending minus tax revenue in a year. The national debt is the accumulated total borrowed. Debt is often compared with GDP, because a larger economy can carry more debt. A tax cut multiplier is smaller than a spending multiplier: tax multiplier = −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC), as part of a tax change is saved.

Critics of deficit spending worry about crowding out private investment, interest costs and burdens on future taxpayers. Supporters argue that in a downturn spending can raise output and incomes, and that debt can fund useful investment. Evidence and values both matter, and economists disagree on the right balance.

example.q: Debt is 600 and GDP 1,000 (billions of zeds). Next year the deficit is 50 and GDP rises to 1,050. What are debt-to-GDP in both years?

analogies.home: A family may borrow to repair a roof that protects its future income, but borrowing for daily needs is riskier.
analogies.farm: A farmer borrowing for a well that raises crops may repay from the extra harvest.
analogies.city: A city builds a rail line today and gains growth later.
analogies.sport: A club spends on youth training hoping for later wins.

stages.mnemonic: Spend or cut taxes to boost; cut spending or raise taxes to cool.
terms: Government spending minus revenue in a year.
A policy that changes automatically with the cycle.

misc.wrong: A government budget works exactly like a household budget.
misc.right: A government can tax, issue its own currency in many cases and has a long horizon, though debt still has costs and limits.

stages.limits: Estimates of multipliers and debt sustainability vary, and countries differ in their ability to borrow. This lesson does not recommend a policy.

Raising income taxes

50 billion
10 billion
8 billion

o: they rise in downturns, supporting spending, without new laws
they cut spending in recessions, which deepens the downturn

taxes fall, so people have more to spend and invest
exports rise, so firms earn more and invest more
banks close, so firms lose their lenders
questions.why: Competition for funds can push up borrowing costs.

questions.q: Match each concept to its meaning.
questions.why: Key fiscal vocabulary.

questions.q: Give one argument for and one against the government running a deficit during a recession.
questions.model: For: extra spending can support demand and jobs when private spending is weak. Against: borrowing raises debt and interest costs and may crowd out private investment or burden future taxpayers.
questions.why: Both sides have merit.

questions.q: Debt grows 3% a year while GDP grows 5% a year. What happens to debt-to-GDP over time?
o: It falls
It rises
It stays the same
It doubles
questions.why: The denominator grows faster than the numerator.

panel.q: Two governments have the same debt ratio but one borrows in its own currency and the other in a foreign currency. Which statement is fair?
o: Foreign-currency borrowing can carry extra risk because the currency must be earned or bought
Their risk is identical, so the currency makes no difference
Debt is never risky for any government
Borrowing in your own currency means you can never face any limits
panel.why: Currency of borrowing affects vulnerability.

panel.q: Why do economists disagree about the effects of austerity (cuts to spending to reduce deficits)?
panel.model: If multipliers are large, cuts can shrink output and worsen the debt ratio. If cuts boost confidence or cut interest rates, the effects may be milder. The outcome depends on circumstances and evidence is contested.
panel.why: The result depends on context.

panel.q: Is borrowing for infrastructure the same as borrowing for current spending?
o: Not necessarily: investment that raises future output may help repay debt, while current spending does not
They are identical in effect, so there is no need to tell them apart
Neither one affects output in the economy, however it is used
Both always pay for themselves in the long run
panel.why: The use of funds matters.

teach.model: Fiscal policy means the government changing its spending and taxes to influence the economy. Spending more or cutting taxes boosts demand, and the reverse cools it. A deficit adds to the national debt, so people debate how much to borrow. For example, a deficit of 50 on debt of 600 raises debt to 650.

stages.title: International trade
stages.hook: If a country can make everything cheaper than its neighbour, why might it still gain from trading with it?
explain: Comparative advantage says a country should specialise in what it produces at the lower opportunity cost and trade for the rest, even if another country is better at everything. Trade can raise total output and lower prices, and gives consumers more variety.

Trade barriers include tariffs (taxes on imports), quotas (limits on quantity) and subsidies. A tariff raises the domestic price, protects domestic producers and raises government revenue, but harms consumers and reduces total surplus. Governments justify barriers by pointing to infant industries, national security or jobs, while economists examine whether other tools would work better.

Gains from trade are shared unevenly. Consumers and export industries often gain while workers in import-competing industries may lose jobs. The terms of trade (export price index ÷ import price index × 100) show whether a country can buy more or fewer imports per unit of exports.

example.q: Country A makes 6 cloth or 3 wheat per worker-day. Country B makes 2 cloth or 2 wheat. Which has comparative advantage in cloth?
steps: A gives up less wheat per cloth, so A has the comparative advantage in cloth (B in wheat).
example.a: Country A in cloth (0.5 wheat vs 1 wheat)

analogies.farm: A farmer good at both milking and fixing tractors may still hire a mechanic to save her own time.
analogies.sport: A star who is the best at everything may still let a teammate take certain roles.
analogies.sea: A fishing nation exports fish and imports machinery.
analogies.music: A conductor who plays every instrument still leaves parts to musicians.

stages.mnemonic: Compare the cost of giving up, not who is best.
terms: Producing at a lower opportunity cost.
A limit on the quantity of an import.
Export price index divided by import price index, times 100.

misc.wrong: A tariff makes the foreign country pay.
misc.right: A tariff is paid by importers and typically passes partly to domestic buyers; the foreign exporter may also lose sales.

stages.limits: Standard trade theory assumes full employment and frictionless adjustment. Economists also debate protection for new industries and the distribution of gains and losses.

trip.prompt: Find the Ricardo example and the assumptions behind it.

questions.q: Comparative advantage is based on...
o: lower opportunity cost
higher total output only
lower wages only
bigger factories
questions.why: What matters is the relative cost of giving up other goods.

questions.q: Per worker-day, A makes 8 shirts or 4 hats. What is A's opportunity cost of one hat in shirts?
questions.why: 4 hats = 8 shirts, so 1 hat = 2 shirts.

questions.q: A tariff of 3 zeds per unit applies to 40 imported units. How much revenue does the government collect?
Export price index is 120 and import price index is 150. What is the terms of trade?
Terms of trade falling from 100 to 80 means...
o: each unit of exports buys fewer imports
each unit of exports buys more imports than before
trade between the countries has stopped
exports have become free for the buyer
questions.why: Export prices fell relative to import prices.

questions.q: Who typically gains from a tariff?
o: Domestic producers of the protected good and the government
Domestic consumers, who pay less for the good
Foreign exporters, who sell more in the market
Nobody can ever gain from a tariff
questions.why: Higher prices help local sellers and raise revenue, while consumers pay more.

questions.q: Match each trade tool to its description.
questions.why: Different ways governments shape trade.

questions.q: Country X is better at making both goods than Y. Under what condition can trade still benefit both?
o: Their opportunity costs differ
Never, since a country cannot gain from trade if it is better at both goods
Only if country Y is richer than country X
Only if wages in the two countries are equal
questions.why: Different opportunity costs create gains from specialisation.

questions.q: A country protects its new car industry with a tariff. Give one argument for and one argument against.
questions.model: For: a young industry may need time to become competitive, and jobs or security may be protected. Against: consumers pay higher prices, firms may become inefficient and other countries may retaliate.
questions.why: Protection involves trade-offs.

questions.q: Why might workers in an import-competing industry oppose trade liberalisation even if the country gains overall?
o: They may lose jobs and find it hard to retrain
They always gain from trade, so they would favour it
Prices fall to zero, so firms cannot compete
Imports vanish altogether, so no one is affected
questions.why: Gains and losses are distributed unevenly.

panel.q: Economists say trade creates winners and losers but net gains. Does that settle whether to liberalise?
o: No, it also depends on whether winners compensate losers and on values about fairness
Yes, completely, since net gains settle every question
No, because the gains from trade are zero
Yes, because the losers do not matter in the sum
panel.why: Net gains do not guarantee fair outcomes without policy.

panel.q: Why might a country that relies heavily on one export be vulnerable?
panel.model: If world prices of its main export fall, national income and jobs suffer. Diversifying exports reduces this risk.
panel.why: Concentration raises exposure to shocks.

panel.q: Why do trade agreements often include rules on subsidies?
o: Subsidies can distort competition between countries
Subsidies are always good for trade and so need no rules
Subsidies lower tariffs to zero for all firms
They have no effect on competition between countries
panel.why: Support for domestic firms can disadvantage foreign competitors.

teach.model: Countries gain by specialising in what they give up least to make and trading for the rest, even if one country is better at everything. A tariff is a tax on imports that protects local firms but raises prices for buyers. Some groups win and some lose from trade. For example, a tariff of 3 on 40 imported units raises 120.

points.ask: How do countries decide what to specialise in?

stages.title: Exchange rates
stages.hook: If the price of one Arbo rises from 2 to 3 Zeds, are Arbo-made goods cheaper or dearer for people in Zedland?
explain: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. In a floating system the rate is set by supply and demand in currency markets; in a fixed or managed system the central bank intervenes to hold it. If demand for a currency rises (more exports, foreign investment, higher interest rates), it appreciates; if it falls, the currency depreciates.

An appreciation makes exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper at home, which tends to reduce net exports; a depreciation does the reverse, though effects take time. Purchasing power parity (PPP) is the idea that the same basket should cost the same across countries once exchange rates are used, so rates tend to move with relative inflation over long periods.

Exchange rates affect inflation, debts denominated in foreign currency and competitiveness. Countries choose regimes by weighing stability against flexibility, and economists disagree about which suits which economy.

example.q: 1 Arbo = 2.5 Zeds. A machine costs 200 Arbos. (a) What does it cost in Zeds? (b) If the Arbo depreciates to 2.0 Zeds, what is the percentage change in the Arbo's value, and what is the machine's new price in Zeds?
steps: New price = 200 × 2.0 = 400 Zeds, so the machine is cheaper for Zedland buyers.
example.a: 500 Zeds; Arbo falls 20%; the machine costs 400 Zeds

analogies.city: Swapping currency at a booth is like buying one good with another.
analogies.farm: A fall in the value of a farmer's currency makes her exports cheaper abroad.
analogies.sport: A star player's transfer fee in a stronger currency costs more at home.
analogies.tech: A phone made abroad becomes dearer when your currency weakens.

stages.mnemonic: Strong currency: imports cheap, exports dear. Weak currency: exports cheap, imports dear.
terms: Price of one currency in terms of another.
A currency rises in value in a floating system.
A currency falls in value in a floating system.
The idea that exchange rates adjust so the same goods cost the same everywhere.

misc.wrong: A strong currency is always good for a country.
misc.right: It makes imports cheap but hurts exporters. What is best depends on the situation.

stages.limits: Exchange rates are volatile and hard to forecast, and PPP holds only roughly and over long horizons.

trip.prompt: Find the difference between fixed and floating exchange-rate systems.

questions.q: 1 Arbo = 2.5 Zeds. How many Zeds is 40 Arbos worth?
1 Arbo = 2.5 Zeds. How many Arbos for 500 Zeds?
The Arbo falls from 2.5 Zeds to 2.0 Zeds. What is the percentage fall in the Arbo's value?
A currency depreciates. The usual effect on that country's exports is to make them...
o: cheaper for foreign buyers
dearer for foreign buyers, who must pay more
unchanged in price, whatever the exchange rate does
unavailable to foreign buyers altogether
questions.why: Foreigners need less of their currency to buy the same goods.

questions.q: Which is most likely to cause a currency to appreciate?
o: Higher interest rates attracting foreign investors
A flood of imports that cuts demand for the currency
A fall in demand for the country's exports
A loss of investor confidence in the economy
questions.why: Investors need the currency to buy local assets, raising demand.

questions.q: In a floating exchange-rate system the rate is set by...
o: supply and demand in currency markets
a fixed legal decree that sets the rate once and for all
the weight of the coins in each country
the tariffs that each country has placed on imports
questions.why: Market forces determine it.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Same basket should cost the same abroad
questions.why: Exchange-rate vocabulary.

questions.q: Explain why a depreciation might not immediately improve a country's trade balance.
questions.model: Trade volumes respond slowly because contracts and habits take time to change, and imports become more expensive at first. The balance can worsen before it improves, depending on how responsive quantities are.
questions.why: Adjustment takes time (the J-curve idea).

questions.q: Country A's inflation is much higher than Country B's for years. According to PPP, A's currency tends to...
o: depreciate against B's
appreciate against B's
stay constant
vanish
questions.why: Higher inflation erodes a currency's purchasing power.

questions.q: A firm borrowed in a foreign currency and its own currency then depreciates. What happens to its debt burden?
o: It rises in local-currency terms
It falls in local-currency terms, since the loan is in foreign money
It disappears, as the loan is repaid by the change
It is unchanged, since the foreign sum owed is the same
questions.why: More local currency is needed to repay.

panel.q: Some economists favour floating rates; others favour fixed rates. What best captures the debate?
o: Floating gives flexibility and independent policy, fixing gives stability and credibility, and each has risks
One is always right, so the debate has an answer
Exchange rates do not matter to any economy
Fixed rates never break, whatever happens to the economy
panel.why: The choice involves trade-offs and depends on the country.

panel.q: Why might a rapid fall in a currency harm ordinary households even if it helps exporters?
panel.model: A weaker currency makes imported goods such as fuel and food dearer, raising the cost of living and inflation, and it can cut real wages and raise foreign-currency debts.
panel.why: Gains and costs are spread unevenly.

panel.q: Why does PPP not hold exactly in the short run?
o: Transport costs, taxes, non-traded services and market frictions differ
Currency markets are closed in the short run
All goods are exactly the same in every country
Prices never change in any country
panel.why: Real-world frictions create gaps.

teach.model: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in another. In a floating system it moves with supply and demand. When a currency depreciates, exports become cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home. For example, if 1 Arbo falls from 2.5 to 2.0 Zeds, a 200-Arbo machine falls from 500 to 400 Zeds.

points.ask: What happens when a currency weakens?

stages.title: Financial markets
stages.hook: A company needs money to build a factory and savers have money to spare. How do financial markets connect them, and what risks are involved?
explain: Financial markets channel savings to borrowers. Firms can borrow by issuing bonds (a loan to the issuer paid back with interest) or raise money by issuing shares (part ownership). Prices in these markets reflect what buyers and sellers expect about future payments and risk.

The present value of a future payment is its value today after discounting: PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)^n. When market interest rates rise, existing bond prices fall, because new bonds pay more. A bond's yield rises as its price falls. Higher expected return usually comes with higher risk, and spreading money across many assets (diversification) can lower risk without removing it.

Financial markets help allocate capital and share risk, but they can also amplify booms and busts through herd behaviour and borrowing. This lesson explains how markets work and is not advice about what to buy.

example.q: A bond pays 50 zeds a year on a face value of 1,000. (a) What is the coupon rate? (b) If its market price falls to 800, what is the current yield? (c) What is the present value of 1,100 zeds due in one year at 10%?

analogies.home: Lending a friend money for a bike with the promise of repayment is like buying a bond.
analogies.farm: Owning a share of a cooperative farm gives you a part of its profits.
analogies.city: A stock exchange is like a market place for pieces of companies.
analogies.sport: Buying a stake in a club is like buying shares: you share good and bad results.

stages.mnemonic: Bonds are loans, shares are ownership; when rates rise, old bond prices fall.
terms: A loan to a borrower paid back with interest.
A unit of ownership in a company.
Income as a percentage of price.
Spreading money across different assets to reduce risk.

misc.wrong: A higher return is always better.
misc.right: Higher expected returns usually come with higher risk, so what is suitable depends on risk and time horizon.

stages.limits: Models of financial markets are imperfect and past performance does not predict the future. This is education, not investment advice.

trip.prompt: Find the difference between bond markets and stock markets.

questions.q: A bond is...
o: a loan to the issuer repaid with interest
a share of ownership in the company
a kind of tax paid to the government
a fee charged by a bank for keeping an account
questions.why: Bondholders are lenders.

questions.q: A share represents...
o: part ownership of a company
a loan to a company that is repaid with interest
a tax paid on income from investments
an insurance contract that pays out after a loss
questions.why: Shareholders are owners.

questions.q: What is the present value of 1,210 zeds due in one year at a 10% discount rate?
What is the present value of 1,210 zeds due in two years at 10% a year (compounded)?
A bond pays 60 zeds a year and its price is 750. What is the current yield in %?
Market interest rates rise. What typically happens to the price of an existing fixed-rate bond?
o: It falls
It rises
It stays fixed
It doubles
questions.why: New bonds pay more, so old ones are worth less.

questions.q: Match each concept to its meaning.
questions.why: Basic finance vocabulary.

questions.q: Explain why investors usually require a higher expected return for riskier assets.
questions.model: Since riskier assets could lose value, investors need the chance of a higher return as compensation. Otherwise they would choose safer assets with similar returns.
questions.why: Return reflects risk.

questions.q: Why does diversification reduce risk?
o: Different assets often do not fall together
It guarantees a profit whenever it is used
It removes all risk, so nothing can be lost
It raises the prices of every asset held
questions.why: Losses on some assets can be offset, but market-wide risk remains.

questions.q: Why can financial markets sometimes amplify booms and busts?
o: Borrowing and herd behaviour can feed rising and falling prices
Prices never change, so there are no booms or busts
Markets are closed for long periods
Only governments trade in financial markets, so they cause it
questions.why: Feedback loops and leverage magnify swings.

panel.q: A friend says a stock that rose last year will surely rise again. What is the best response?
o: Past returns do not guarantee future returns; prices depend on expectations of the future
They are certainly right, since a rising stock keeps rising
Stocks only ever fall, so the friend is wrong in any case
Past returns are the only guide that a buyer needs
panel.why: Markets are uncertain.

panel.q: Why is it important to have rules and regulators for banks and markets?
panel.model: Rules protect savers and investors from fraud, promote trust and transparent information, and reduce the risk that failures spread through the system and cause a crisis.
panel.why: Finance depends on trust and stability.

panel.q: If discount rates rise, the present value of a fixed future payment...
o: falls
rises
stays the same
becomes negative
panel.why: Dividing by a bigger number gives a smaller value.

teach.model: A bond is a loan that pays interest and a share is part ownership of a company. A payment in the future is worth less today, so we discount it. When market interest rates rise, old bond prices fall. Higher return usually comes with higher risk. For example, 1,100 due in a year at 10% is worth 1,000 today.

points.ask: How are risk and return linked?

stages.title: Economic development
stages.hook: Two countries have the same total GDP growth, but in one most people see their lives improve while in the other few do. Why?
explain: Economic development means improving living standards, health, education and freedom, not only raising income. The Human Development Index (HDI) combines life expectancy, education and income. Growth in GDP per person is approximately GDP growth minus population growth.

Development depends on many factors: institutions and rule of law, education and health, infrastructure, investment, technology, trade and geography. Countries differ in history, and some face debt, conflict or climate shocks. Economists debate causes; there is no single recipe, and policies that work in one setting may fail in another.

Inequality is measured using tools like the Gini coefficient (0 = equal, 1 = one person has everything) and poverty lines. Choices about aid, trade, borrowing and industrial policy involve trade-offs and different views. Development should be judged by how people's lives change, with their own voices and priorities.

example.q: A country's GDP grows 5% and its population grows 2%. What is the approximate growth of GDP per person? If it started at 2,000 zeds per person, roughly how much is it after a year?
example.a: About 3%, giving about 2,060 zeds per person

analogies.farm: Irrigation, schooling and roads together help a farming region more than any one alone.
analogies.city: A city grows richer when it has schools, clean water and reliable power.
analogies.nature: A forest thrives when soil, water and light all work together.
analogies.tech: Mobile payments help people without bank branches save and trade.

stages.mnemonic: Development is about lives, not just totals: health, learning, income, freedom.
terms: Improvement in people's wellbeing, including health, education and income.
Index combining life expectancy, education and income.
Measure of inequality from 0 (equal) to 1 (maximum inequality).
Rules and organisations that shape economic behaviour.

misc.wrong: There is one proven path every country should follow.
misc.right: Evidence shows different countries succeeded with different mixes, and context matters.

stages.limits: Development indicators simplify. Economists disagree about the importance of institutions, aid, trade and geography, and measures like HDI leave out many things that people value.

trip.prompt: Find the three components of HDI and how countries are grouped.

questions.q: The HDI combines...
o: life expectancy, education and income
GDP, debt and trade
population, area and rainfall
taxes, government spending and inflation
questions.why: These are the three dimensions.

questions.q: GDP grows 6% and population grows 2.5%. What is the approximate growth of GDP per person in %?
GDP per person is 3,000 zeds and grows 4% for one year. What is it after one year?
A Gini coefficient of 0 means...
o: perfect equality
maximum inequality
no GDP
no population
questions.why: Everyone has the same income.

questions.q: A country's GDP per person rises but life expectancy and school attendance do not. What does this suggest?
o: Growth alone may not improve wellbeing
Development is complete, since income is higher
The HDI must have risen, since income has gone up
Income is irrelevant to development
questions.why: Income gains may not reach health and education.

questions.q: Which is an example of an 'institution' in development economics?
o: A reliable legal system protecting property and contracts
A tractor that is used on a farm
A river that runs through the country
A coin that is used in markets
questions.why: Institutions are rules and organisations.

questions.q: Match each factor to how it can help development.
pairs: Lowers costs of moving goods and people
Gives confidence to invest and trade
Improves ability to work and learn
questions.why: Several factors work together.

questions.q: Explain why using only GDP per person to judge development can be misleading.
questions.model: GDP per person is an average, so it can hide inequality, and it leaves out health, education, freedom and environmental harm that also shape people's lives.
questions.why: A single number cannot capture wellbeing.

questions.q: A country spends heavily on one export crop and its price collapses. Which lesson about development is illustrated?
o: Diversification can reduce vulnerability to price shocks
Specialisation is always safe, however prices move
Prices never fall for an export crop
Exports do not matter to a country's development
questions.why: Over-dependence on one commodity is risky.

questions.q: Order these steps as a simple chain linking education to higher income.
questions.why: Education raises human capital, productivity and pay, though other factors also matter.

panel.q: Economists disagree on whether foreign aid helps development. What best summarises the evidence?
o: Results vary by type of aid, context and governance, and the debate is unsettled
Aid always works, so the debate is settled
Aid never works, so the debate is settled
Nobody has ever studied the effects of aid
panel.why: The evidence is mixed and context-dependent.

panel.q: Why should people affected by development projects have a say in them?
panel.model: Local people know their needs and priorities, so involving them leads to better and fairer projects, and respects their rights and dignity.
panel.why: Participation improves relevance and fairness.

panel.q: Is it possible for a country to grow fast while inequality rises?
o: Yes, growth and inequality can move in different directions
No, never, since growth lifts everyone equally
Only in small countries, never in large ones
Only if prices in the country are falling
panel.why: Average growth says nothing about distribution.

teach.model: Economic development means people's lives improving in health, education and income, not just GDP rising. GDP per person grows roughly at GDP growth minus population growth. Many factors matter, including schools, health, institutions and infrastructure, and no single recipe works everywhere. For example, 5% GDP growth with 2% population growth gives about 3% growth per person.

points.ask: How do you work out GDP per person growth?
